cards.front: What is React Native?
cards.back: A framework that lets you write an app in React and JavaScript or TypeScript and render real native views on iOS and Android, instead of HTML in a web view.

cards.front: What are View and Text?
cards.back: View is the basic layout container, like a div. Text is the only component that can render strings. A raw string inside a View is an error.

cards.front: How do you make something tappable?
cards.back: Wrap it in Pressable (or a Touchable component) and handle onPress. Pressable also gives you pressed state for feedback and supports hitSlop to grow the touch area.

cards.front: What does StyleSheet.create do?
cards.back: It declares style objects once, outside render, and validates them in development. Styles are plain objects with camelCase keys and unitless numbers, not CSS files.

cards.front: What happens when you pass an array to style?
cards.back: The styles are merged left to right, so later entries win. Falsy entries are skipped, which makes conditional styles easy: style={[styles.btn, active && styles.active]}.

cards.front: How does flexbox differ from the web by default?
cards.back: flexDirection defaults to column, not row. alignContent defaults to flex-start, and flexShrink defaults to 0. Every View is a flex container.

cards.front: What unit do React Native sizes use?
cards.back: Unitless numbers in density-independent pixels, so 16 looks about the same size on every screen density. Percentages are allowed as strings, such as width: '50%'.

cards.front: Why use FlatList instead of mapping inside a ScrollView?
cards.back: FlatList virtualises: it renders only the rows near the viewport and recycles the rest out of memory. A ScrollView renders every child up front, which is slow and memory hungry for long lists.

cards.front: What is keyExtractor for?
cards.back: It gives each row a stable, unique key so React can match rows across renders. Using the index breaks state and animations when rows are inserted, removed or reordered.

cards.front: When does getItemLayout help?
cards.back: When every row has a known fixed height. FlatList can then skip measuring rows and jump straight to an index with scrollToIndex.

cards.front: When would you choose SectionList?
cards.back: When rows are grouped under headers, such as contacts by letter. It is virtualised like FlatList and supports sticky section headers.

cards.front: What does a stack navigator do?
cards.back: It keeps a history of screens. Navigating pushes a screen on top, going back pops it. Screens below stay mounted, so their state survives.

cards.front: How should you pass data to a screen?
cards.back: Pass small, serialisable params such as an id, then load the data on that screen. Big objects or functions in params break deep links and state persistence.

cards.front: What is a deep link?
cards.back: A URL such as myapp://orders/42 that opens the app on a specific screen. The navigation linking config maps URL paths to screens and params.

cards.front: What does Platform.select return?
cards.back: The value for the current platform key (ios, android, or another), falling back to default. It is handy for small differences in styles or constants.

cards.front: How do platform-specific files work?
cards.back: Name files Button.ios.tsx and Button.android.tsx and import ./Button. The bundler picks the right file for each platform at build time.

cards.front: How do you handle the Android back button?
cards.back: Subscribe with BackHandler.addEventListener. Return true to say you handled it, or false to let the default go back. Remove the listener when the screen unfocuses.

cards.front: What is JSI?
cards.back: The JavaScript Interface: a C++ layer that lets JavaScript hold references to native objects and call them directly, even synchronously, instead of sending JSON messages over the old asynchronous bridge.

cards.front: What are Fabric and TurboModules?
cards.back: Parts of the new architecture. Fabric is the new renderer, built on JSI, that can render synchronously when needed. TurboModules are native modules loaded lazily and called through JSI.

cards.front: What does Hermes bring?
cards.back: A JavaScript engine tuned for mobile. It compiles JavaScript to bytecode at build time, which cuts startup time and memory use.

cards.front: Which threads matter in a React Native app?
cards.back: The JavaScript thread runs your React code. The UI (main) thread draws native views and handles touches. Layout is calculated off the JS thread. A busy JS thread makes taps and JS-driven animations lag.

cards.front: When do you need a native module?
cards.back: When JavaScript cannot reach a platform feature you need, such as a device sensor or a platform SDK. You write the native side and expose a typed interface to JavaScript.

cards.front: What does codegen do in the new architecture?
cards.back: It reads a typed spec file for a native module or component and generates the native interface code, so JavaScript and native agree on types at build time.

cards.front: Why remove native event listeners?
cards.back: Each subscription keeps a callback alive. If a screen unmounts without calling remove(), you leak memory and may call setState on an unmounted screen.

cards.front: What is async key-value storage good for, and not good for?
cards.back: Small, non-secret data such as preferences or cached lists, stored as strings. It is not encrypted, so never put tokens or passwords in it.

cards.front: Where should you keep auth tokens?
cards.back: In the platform secure store (Keychain on iOS, Keystore-backed storage on Android), through a secure storage library. It encrypts data at rest.

cards.front: Does fetch time out by itself?
cards.back: No. Use an AbortController with a timer to abort slow requests, and clear the timer when the request finishes.

cards.front: What does offline-first mean?
cards.back: The app reads from local data first and queues writes while offline, then syncs when the network returns. Writes need idempotency keys so retries do not create duplicates.

cards.front: What does useNativeDriver: true do?
cards.back: It sends the animation to the UI thread up front, so it keeps running smoothly even if the JS thread is busy. It only works for non-layout props such as transform and opacity.

cards.front: What does interpolate do?
cards.back: It maps an input range to an output range, such as scroll offset 0–100 to opacity 1–0. Use extrapolate: 'clamp' to stop values going past the ends.

cards.front: What is the frame budget at 60 fps?
cards.back: About 16.7 ms per frame. If JavaScript work takes longer, frames drop and the app feels janky.

cards.front: How do you stop list rows re-rendering?
cards.back: Wrap the row component in React.memo and keep its props stable: useCallback for handlers and no new inline objects or arrays on each render.

cards.front: What does AppState tell you?
cards.back: Whether the app is active, in the background, or (on iOS) inactive during transitions. Listen for changes to pause work, refresh data or lock sensitive screens.

cards.front: How should you ask for a permission?
cards.back: Ask at the moment the feature needs it and explain why. If the user has blocked it permanently, you cannot ask again, so offer a link to the app settings.

cards.front: How should components be tested?
cards.back: Render them in Jest with a testing library and query by what the user sees: role, label or text. Fire events such as press, then assert on the visible result.

cards.front: Why mock native modules in unit tests?
cards.back: Unit tests run in Node with no device, so native modules do not exist. Mock them to return fixed values and test your JavaScript logic.

cards.front: What can an over-the-air update change?
cards.back: Only the JavaScript bundle and assets. Any change to native code, native dependencies or permissions needs a new store build.

cards.front: Why must the build number go up for every store upload?
cards.back: Stores reject an upload with a build number they have already seen. The user-facing version can stay the same, but the build number must increase.

cards.front: What do accessibilityLabel and accessibilityRole do?
cards.back: The label is what a screen reader reads for the element. The role says what it is, such as button or header, so users know how to interact with it.

cards.front: What is Expo, and when would you go bare?
cards.back: An open-source framework and tooling around React Native that handles native config, builds and updates. Go bare when you need full control of the native projects and can maintain them.
